In *MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents* [[1]](#ref-1) (arXiv, February 2, 2026), Haozhen Zhang et al. (Nanyang Technological University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Chicago, and Tsinghua University) reframe LLM-agent memory operations as a learnable, evolving skill bank. An RL-trained *controller* selects skills for the current *span* — a contiguous segment of the interaction trace, typically covering multiple turns, that the *executor* consumes as input to a single LLM call. An LLM *designer* then periodically rewrites the bank from hard training cases.

> Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present *MemSkill*, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a *controller* that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based *executor* that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a *designer* that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents.

## Methods

- Two banks anchor the system, with three components alternating around them.
  - **Skill bank** — a shared, slowly evolving library of memory *skills*: structured templates, each with a short description, a "when to use" condition, a "how to apply" procedure, and constraints. The executor consumes a selected subset as guidance for one LLM call over a text span. It starts from four primitives (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SKIP`) and grows as training proceeds.
  - **Memory bank** — per-trace: the running set of extracted memories the executor accumulates and rewrites for a single interaction. Updated every span.
- The **controller** (a lightweight multilayer perceptron over a shared encoder) scores each skill in the current skill bank by dot-product between a state embedding $h_t = f_{ctx}(x_t, M_t)$ and a per-skill embedding $u_i = f_{skill}(\text{desc}(s_i))$, then selects an ordered Top-$K$ set without replacement. Here $x_t$ is the current span, $M_t$ the memories retrieved from the trace's memory bank, $\text{desc}(s_i)$ the natural-language description of skill $s_i$ in the skill bank, and $f_{ctx}$, $f_{skill}$ are the two heads sharing an encoder backbone.
- The **executor** (a frozen LLM) applies the selected skills in one pass to update the trace's memory bank.
- The **designer** (also a frozen LLM) periodically mines a sliding hard-case buffer, clusters the failures, and proposes refinements to existing skills or new skills — edits that land in the skill bank, not the memory bank.
- Controller training:
  - **Algorithm.** PPO [[2]](#ref-2) with downstream task reward (F1, success rate, etc.) as the optimization signal.
  - **Top-$K$ sampling.** Selecting an ordered Top-$K$ set without replacement factorizes the joint log-probability via the standard sequential rule, so PPO can score the whole subset selection.
  - **Rollback on regression.** Snapshots roll back if a skill-bank update degrades training reward, so a bad designer edit can't poison the policy.
  - **Exploration bias.** After each evolution step, exploration is briefly biased toward newly introduced skills, giving them a fair chance at being selected before low scores filter them out.

## Results

- **Setup.** Four benchmarks — LoCoMo [[3]](#ref-3) and LongMemEval [[4]](#ref-4) for conversational memory, ALFWorld [[5]](#ref-5) for embodied tasks, and HotpotQA [[6]](#ref-6) for cross-distribution skill transfer. Two base LLMs: LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct. MemSkill is trained only on LLaMA; Qwen and LongMemEval results are zero-shot transfers of the learned skill bank.
- **Main comparison (Table 1 below).** Across the two base-model blocks, MemSkill leads every benchmark; ▲ marks settings evaluated by pure transfer (no training on that base model or dataset), and bold marks the best score within each block.
  - LLaMA block: LLM-judge average 55.19 against the strongest baseline at 42.23 (A-MEM), with ALFWorld success rates of 47.86 / 47.01 on seen / unseen splits versus 40.71 / 38.06 for the runners-up. (LLM-judge: a separate LLM scores each predicted answer against the gold answer for semantic match — the headline metric for open-ended conversational QA, where token-level F1 misses semantic equivalence.)
  - Qwen transfer (zero-shot): ALFWorld 60.00 / 64.18 success rates without any retraining, against ~57 / 54 for CoN.

![Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="table1-full.png"}

- **Component ablations (Table 2 below).** On LoCoMo (LLM-judge), removing the controller drops LLaMA from 50.96 to 45.86 and Qwen from 52.07 to 41.24; removing the designer drops them to 44.11 and 34.71. The Qwen gap is bigger, suggesting the evolved skill bank carries most of the cross-model transfer benefit; the controller policy alone doesn't transfer as well.

![Table 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table2.png){fig-align="center"}

- **Distribution-shift transfer (Figure 3 below).** The LoCoMo-trained skill bank is ported to long-document QA on HotpotQA at three concatenation budgets — no HotpotQA-specific training; the controller scores from the LoCoMo-trained bank with $K$ varied at test time. MemSkill at $K=7$ holds the lead at every budget, but the gap to lower $K$ widens as documents pile up — at 200 docs, $K=7$ scores 66.80 while $K=3$ drops to 58.20.

![Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure3.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **Operator-level evolution.** The closest learning-based siblings, Memory-R1 [[7]](#ref-7) and Mem-α [[8]](#ref-8), both RL-train memory management against downstream task signals, but with a fixed primitive set (add/update/delete/skip and friends). MemSkill's contribution is that the **skill bank itself is learnable**: the four primitives (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SKIP`) serve as starter templates rather than a frozen action set. The designer can refine those starting templates *and* add brand-new skills written from scratch as natural-language templates for failure modes the bank doesn't yet cover. The controller adapts because skills are scored by description-embedding rather than a fixed action head. The cross-model transfer ablation supports the reading: most of the Qwen-side gain (52.07 → 34.71 without designer) comes from the evolved bank rather than the controller policy.
- **The "skill" abstraction here is not a callable.** In the [Anthropic Skills](/posts/20251124-skills-not-software-engineering/) sense, a skill is a packaged routine the agent invokes with explicit arguments and a return value; the [API/Tool/Skill ladder](/posts/20260414-api-mcp-tool-skill/) treats it as the layer where judgment and sequencing live. MemSkill's "skills" don't take per-skill arguments. They all share the same implicit context (the current span and retrieved memories), and the executor combines the selected $K$ as joint guidance for a single LLM call. They're closer to selection priors and prompt fragments than to callable routines. The gains here come from learning over a discrete library of prompt fragments under shared context, rather than from a calling protocol.
- **LLM-as-designer is a recurring outer-loop pattern.** The closed-loop alternation between (a) RL-training a learner and (b) using a frozen LLM to rewrite the design space from clustered failure cases is the same recipe as ADAS [[9]](#ref-9) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-adas/ --> for agent scaffolds and AlphaEvolve [[10]](#ref-10) for algorithms. MemSkill is the operator-level instance of that pattern. By the framework in [Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/), this is still extrinsic metacognition: the loop's structure (when to evolve, how to cluster, what counts as a hard case) is human-defined, and only the operators inside it adapt. A genuine intrinsic version would let the agent decide when its skill bank needs rewriting, instead of running on a fixed schedule.
- **"Self-evolving" overstates test-time behavior.** Both the controller and the skill bank are trained **offline** and **frozen at deployment**; only the per-trace memory content updates online during interaction. The evolution described in the title refers to a training-phase alternation between controller updates and designer rewrites, rather than test-time adaptation.
- **Memory items aren't shown directly.** The paper describes the memory bank abstractly as $M_t$ (up to 20 retrieved per span via Contriever, so text-based) but never includes a worked example of an actual stored item. The shape has to be reverse-engineered from the skill case studies in Appendix B: dialogue skills produce short factual sentences ("who did what, where, when"), while ALFWorld skills produce structured tuples like (action, constraint) or (object, location, state). Each skill writes items in its own shape, so the bank ends up as a heterogeneous text store with no central schema. The framing of "evolving memory operations" is harder to picture concretely without seeing what those operations produce. Figure 4's case study (below) shows evolved *skills* rather than the *memory bank* they generate.

![Figure 4 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure4.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure4-full.png"}

- **Skill transfer has a budget-sensitive ceiling.** HotpotQA complicates the generalization story: the LoCoMo-trained bank does port to long-document QA, but the gap between $K=7$ and $K=3$ widens sharply at 200 docs (66.80 vs 58.20). At 50 and 100 docs the two are within ~3 points, while the dialogue benchmarks were fine at $K=3$. Skills evolved on dialogue traces don't cover long-document QA well at low $K$. At 200 docs concatenated, you need to fire a larger fraction of the bank to find enough applicable skills. The "reusable skills" claim is more conditional than the headline reads: portable when the inference-time budget matches, less so under shift.
